navigation.strategy: Read one linked reference at a time; follow relevant branches, never recursively expand the tree.

page.boundary: one section = one compositional learning page; no authored section type
page.focus: one main visual/activity plus supporting text; advisory warnings
page.presentation: hands-free automatic scenes/beats; mode-specific views of shared content

selectionGuidance:
Learning-first, representation-aware authoring: learning objective → knowledge structure → learner action → candidate section capabilities → representation and configuration → focused contracts → OUI and narration → validation/repair → delivery. Choose the simplest representation or complementary combination that fully supports the intended learning experience. Text, layouts, visuals and prebuilt activities share one catalog; there is no section ranking, visual quota or mandatory sequence.

Compare candidates by knowledge fidelity (preserve information and relationships), learner action (what the learner does), perspective coverage (what additional views reveal), cognitive clarity (avoid unnecessary complexity), assessment suitability (what response demonstrates the outcome) and authoring feasibility (what the evidence can actually model). Record the choice in TopicPlan activity, rationale and presentation.strategy before retrieving exact signatures. Resolve relevant advisory warnings or explicitly justify proceeding; structural validity alone is not experience readiness.

Bullets teach numbered linear procedures, checklists, prerequisites, key points, supporting details and concise summaries. The knowledge itself should fit a list; moving paragraphs into bullet items is not a representation decision. For visual subjects, proactively compose informative images with cards and text, and include learner-visible references beside researched or time-sensitive claims. Images and links support the same learning unit; they are not separate page types. Read contracts/media-composition.md (installed skills: references/planning/media-composition.md) for composition examples. Compare compositions proactively: matched attributes in a table, verified use-case examples in cards, spatial mechanisms in labelled Svg, and measured quantities in charts. Simplest means clearest for the learner, not fewest component types or easiest syntax. Steps add visual stage guidance; Flowchart teaches interactions, responsibilities, messages, data or states, even in a linear process when perspectives add understanding. Reflection Sequence practises order; User Journey follows a person's experience. Text is appropriate for connected prose, nuanced explanation and argument; consider alternatives when they clarify the objective, without forcing interactivity.

Flashcards introduce definitions and meanings as well as practise recall. Cards/stacks compare examples, tables compare factual attributes, labelled Svg diagrams explain spatial structure, and charts explain quantities or trends. Empirical charts require supplied or verified data; clearly label illustrative data and never invent benchmark results. Tradeoff Sandbox explains comparisons as well as contextual decisions; Formula Sandbox explores parameter sensitivity. Select other prebuilt activities by their learning purpose below.

For a 3D web research lesson, compare matched capabilities in a Table, inspect annotated use-case cards, and explain camera/geometry with a labelled Svg when each serves an objective. Bullets can guide real initialization steps; Flowchart can trace system messages. These are candidates, not a required section mix.

For full lessons, combine sections only when each adds a distinct contribution: e.g. Flowchart explains RAG tool execution, Bullets guides implementation, Scenario explores retrieval failures and Quiz assesses application. Distinguish presentation, exploration and assessment. Viewing, clicking, switching views and flipping cards are engagement, not demonstrated mastery.

Read only plausible capability summaries, then the exact contracts and required model dependencies of the selected components. Prebuilt activities package reusable interactions and presentation scenes; select them by fit, just like tables, text or controls. If a contract is unavailable, correct the path or explicitly revise and revalidate the plan; never silently downgrade to prose or invent signatures. Generic child alternatives are choices, not dependencies.

visualChoices.components: AreaChart; use cumulative data when teaching accumulation

visualChoices.components: ScatterChart; an association alone does not establish causation

visualChoices.components: Table for a compact overview; TradeoffSandbox for an explained comparison

components.summary: Topic opener: what it is, why it matters, and a roadmap of the sections ahead. `displayTitle` overrides the title shown inside the card.

teaching.introduces: Orient the learner through the topic’s purpose, significance and roadmap.
teaching.exploration: Connect the opening question and motivation to the upcoming learning activities.
teaching.evidence: Viewing, opening or selecting is engagement; ask for an observable explanation or application when the objective requires evidence.
teaching.limits: Keep orientation focused and grounded. Intro is a prebuilt option alongside text and cards, not a mandatory first page or evidence of understanding.

components.mentalModel: Orientation, purpose and roadmap
components.selectionQuestion: What will I learn, why does it matter, and where are we going?

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Read the purpose and roadmap.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Orient attention; keep the opening focused.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Reading is engagement, not demonstrated understanding.

components.summary: Linear instructions, prerequisites, checklists, key points and summaries; set `ordered` true for numbered procedures.

teaching.introduces: Teach procedures: executing instructions, understanding step connections or checking prerequisites.
teaching.exploration: Choose Steps for explained instructions, Bullets for concise checklists and Flowchart for meaningful sequence, dependencies, branches or responsibilities.
teaching.evidence: Following a demonstration or clicking a checklist does not prove procedural skill. ReflectionSequence can check an already-taught order when appropriate.
teaching.limits: A linear procedure can justify a diagram; follow the actual selected contract and never invent participants or events to activate Flowchart. No particular mix of these components is required.

components.mentalModel: Linear procedures, prerequisites, checklists and key points
components.selectionQuestion: Is the task a linear procedure, checklist, key points or summary? Preserve comparative, spatial and relational structure when a table or diagram teaches it better.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Follow numbered instructions, check prerequisites or inspect key points and supporting details.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Use documented item beats; avoid turning every item into a paragraph wall.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: A checklist presentation does not demonstrate procedural skill.

components.summary: Introduce and explore meaningful categories with defining features, examples, scope and distinctions. Explain overlaps when relevant; browsing alone is not classification evidence.

teaching.introduces: Introduce and organize meaningful kinds with defining features, examples and distinctions, including first encounters with a domain.
teaching.exploration: Inspect category scopes and shared or distinguishing features; explain overlaps where they exist.
teaching.evidence: Browsing is exploration; classification evidence requires an observable learner response.
teaching.limits: The current category browser is flat. Do not invent nested category fields or force mutually exclusive groups. Use ConceptMap for relationships and DecisionTree for identification rules.

components.mentalModel: Classification and distinctions
components.selectionQuestion: What kinds exist, what defines them, and how do I recognise their differences? Introduce meaningful categories with examples and explain overlaps; use relationships only when the subject supports them.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Discover kinds, inspect examples and distinguish categories, including explained overlaps.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Use focused category beats instead of a dense classification dump.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Category exploration is engagement, not a classification test.

components.summary: Gallery of captioned images.

teaching.introduces: Teach visual recognition and concrete examples by showing relevant features, variations and distinctions.
teaching.exploration: Inspect and compare images with explanatory labels or captions; use the selected gallery’s actual preview and presentation behavior.
teaching.evidence: Viewing, zooming or switching images is engagement. Recognition evidence requires a response that identifies or explains a feature.
teaching.limits: Check the MCP runtime image policy: a reachable HTTPS URL may still be blocked. Images must contribute to the learning goal, remain legible and use supported accessibility/attribution fields. Do not infer hidden mechanisms from a photograph or claim a gallery provides a classification test.

components.mentalModel: Visual recognition and concrete references
components.selectionQuestion: What does it look like? Compare examples, textures, objects or screenshots.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Inspect and compare visual examples.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Check image labels and legibility at the actual viewport.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Visual inspection alone does not establish recognition accuracy.

components.summary: Layer-stack map: layers as rows (foundation last), blocks placed on a gap-free grid. Give blocks `dependsOn` so readers can tap a block to trace what it needs and what it affects. `displayTitle` overrides the title shown inside the map.

teaching.introduces: Explain foundations, layered responsibilities and what builds on or is supported by what.
teaching.exploration: Inspect foundations, layers and meaningful peer groups; Present derives focused scenes from the authored stack.
teaching.evidence: Viewing, opening or selecting is engagement; ask for an observable explanation or application when the objective requires evidence.
teaching.limits: Layers must express defensible foundations or dependencies. Do not stack unrelated categories for decoration or infer process order from vertical placement.

components.mentalModel: Layered dependency and foundation
components.selectionQuestion: What builds on or is supported by what? Examples include network layers or cloud foundation → agent runtime → application.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Inspect layers and what each foundation supports.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Keep layer labels short and inspect the complete stack in Read.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Layer inspection alone does not demonstrate dependency reasoning.

components.summary: A person’s experience across product or service stages. Read explores stages; Present walks goals, actions, responses and optional friction and outcomes without an Event Storming diagram.

teaching.introduces: Explain a procedure or experience through a person’s goals, actions, responses and friction; it can introduce a subject through a concrete experience.
teaching.exploration: Inspect stages and their context, identify friction and compare authored improvements; Present guides the journey.
teaching.evidence: Stage selection does not show that the learner can diagnose friction or explain an improvement.
teaching.limits: Keep the person’s experience distinct from internal system execution. Ground claims about users in evidence, or label the journey illustrative. Use Flowchart for system handoffs.

components.mentalModel: A person’s experience with a product or service
components.selectionQuestion: What does the person want, do and experience at each stage, and how can friction be resolved?

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Inspect stages, goals, friction and improvements in a person’s journey.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Focus on one stage at a time; check horizontal content remains reachable.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Stage selection is exploration, not evidence of diagnosing friction.

components.summary: Measured task timeline: one row per activity, sorted by start time, with duration-scaled bars, parallel work and finish-to-start dependencies. Present keeps the whole diagram visible while focusing authored groups.

teaching.introduces: Explain when work happens, measured duration, overlap, dependencies and waiting, including scheduling and performance examples.
teaching.exploration: Inspect authored start times, durations and groups to explain elapsed time and concurrency.
teaching.evidence: Ask the learner to interpret overlap, waiting or completion time; selecting an activity alone is engagement.
teaching.limits: Use verified values or clearly labelled illustrative timings with units. Geometry must follow those values. Sequence order alone does not establish duration or causation.

components.mentalModel: Measured time, duration, overlap and waiting
components.selectionQuestion: When does each task start and finish, what runs together, and what must wait?

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Inspect start times, durations, overlap and waiting.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Time geometry must use authored measurements; verify labels and scale.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Selection is exploration; interpretation needs a learner response.

components.summary: A whole divided into measurable parts: costs, counts, time allocation or conditional probability. Calculates each part’s share of its parent and the whole, validates totals, and explains one split per presentation beat.

teaching.introduces: Explain how a measurable whole divides into parts, or how conditional probability composes along paths.
teaching.exploration: Inspect branches, totals and the contribution of parts; choose the documented quantity or probability model.
teaching.evidence: Expansion alone is engagement; an interpreted contribution or probability calculation can supply evidence when checked.
teaching.limits: Use defensible quantities, units and conditional assumptions. A category hierarchy alone is not a measurable breakdown. Do not invent amounts or probabilities to fill branches.

components.mentalModel: Parts of a measurable whole and conditional probability
components.selectionQuestion: How does a total divide through a hierarchy? Use quantity mode for costs/counts and probability mode for conditional branches and path probabilities.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Explore how a quantity or probability divides through branches.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Preserve visible totals and branch labels; inspect deep trees in Read.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Expansion is engagement; it does not establish quantitative reasoning.

components.summary: Animated Event Storming flowchart. Every actor and system must be used by at least one step.

teaching.introduces: Teach procedures: executing instructions, understanding step connections or checking prerequisites.
teaching.exploration: Choose Steps for explained instructions, Bullets for concise checklists and Flowchart for meaningful sequence, dependencies, branches or responsibilities.
teaching.evidence: Following a demonstration or clicking a checklist does not prove procedural skill. ReflectionSequence can check an already-taught order when appropriate.
teaching.limits: A linear procedure can justify a diagram; follow the actual selected contract and never invent participants or events to activate Flowchart. No particular mix of these components is required.

components.mentalModel: Process, responsibility and interaction
components.selectionQuestion: How do procedure steps connect, depend on one another or branch? What happens, what triggers it, and who handles it? Linear procedures are candidates too; choose a view supported by the actual model.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Step through events, responsibilities and handoffs in the appropriate view.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Select the documented process view and inspect graph labels at the viewport.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Stepping through a process is engagement; test application separately.

views.purpose: Event → policy → command → system → resulting event; explain triggers and rules.
Components, their responsibilities and their connections.
Who sends what to whom, and in what order; vertical spacing is not measured duration.
How events change the state of something.

capabilities.narration: Flowchart.initialView selects the primary view; NarrationStep.view may change views on the same beat for a distinct teaching purpose.
capabilities.modelingConstraints: Use real participants and event → policy → command → handler → event cycles. Data Flow uses Event.data; State Machine requires StateMachine and Event.enters. JourneyStep.processGroup is a phase label, not a state. Never invent model detail to activate views.

components.summary: Branching "what would you do?" scenario. `startNode` defaults to "start". `displayTitle` overrides the title shown inside the scenario.

teaching.introduces: Teach through a concrete situation, decisions, consequences and feedback; a scenario can introduce and explain a concept rather than only test it afterward.
teaching.exploration: Explore authored paths and compare how choices affect outcomes and the lesson each outcome illustrates.
teaching.evidence: Separate exploration from assessment. Outcome ratings are authored judgments, not independently verified real-world performance. Present demonstrates authored content with separate state; demonstrated answers are not learner attempts.
teaching.limits: Explain assumptions and keep consequences plausible and source-supported or labelled illustrative. A branching story is not a simulation of every possible outcome.

components.mentalModel: Consequences across decisions
components.selectionQuestion: What happens if I choose this, then make another decision? Explore authored paths and outcomes.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Choose authored decisions and inspect consequences.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present demonstrates paths; Read permits learner decisions.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: An explored consequence is not independently verified mastery.

components.summary: Explained comparison of alternatives across shared criteria, strengths, limitations and consequences. Use for comparison even without a decision request; contextual situations and recommendations are optional. Qualitative comparisons use empty metrics; avoid invented scores or a universal winner.

teaching.introduces: Explain alternatives across shared criteria, strengths, limitations and consequences, with contextual decision support when useful.
teaching.exploration: Inspect matched options and their implications; optionally compare situations, authored metrics or recommendations.
teaching.evidence: Exploration or choosing an option is engagement; a justified comparison or decision requires an observable response.
teaching.limits: A comparison needs no winner or scores. Use existing empty-metric contracts for qualitative comparisons; recommendations and numerical values must follow explicit assumptions and evidence.

components.mentalModel: Presenting options, comparing alternatives and trade-offs
components.selectionQuestion: What are my options and how do they differ across shared criteria? Explain strengths, limitations and consequences even without a decision request. Contextual suitability and recommendations are optional; no scoring or mathematical optimisation is required.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Compare options across shared criteria and explain strengths, limitations and consequences; optionally explore suitability for a situation.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present guides option comparisons; Read supports learner exploration.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Exploring options does not prove a justified decision.

components.summary: Parameter sandbox: sliders drive live formula-based metrics.

teaching.introduces: Teach an authored input/output relationship through predictions and experiments, including first explanations of a formula.
teaching.exploration: Vary meaningful inputs and interpret outputs, ranges and sensitivity. Explain why the formula responds as it does.
teaching.evidence: Changing a slider alone is engagement. Ask for a prediction, explanation or calculation if evidence is needed. Present demonstrates authored content with separate state; demonstrated answers are not learner attempts.
teaching.limits: State the formula, units, assumptions and valid domain. The sandbox evaluates an authored model, not the real external system; do not present invented scores or correlations as causal measurements.

components.mentalModel: Input–output relationships and sensitivity
components.selectionQuestion: How does changing an input change a calculated result? Let the learner vary inputs to an authored formula.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Vary inputs and observe authored calculated outputs.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present demonstrates chosen inputs; Read is needed for learner experiments.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Slider movement is engagement, not correctness or causal understanding.

components.summary: Interactive decision guide. `root` is the ID of the first node. `displayTitle` overrides the title shown inside the guide.

teaching.introduces: Teach explicit criteria and reasoning behind diagnosis, identification or selection, as well as guiding a decision.
teaching.exploration: Follow authored questions and compare paths, explanations and leaf recommendations.
teaching.evidence: Reaching a leaf is not proof of diagnostic skill or a verified recommendation. Ask the learner to explain the relevant rule when needed.
teaching.limits: Branches must represent defensible explicit rules and reachable outcomes. Preserve the existing question/leaf contract; a diagnostic guide does not establish an empirical probability or universal best choice.

components.mentalModel: Rule-based diagnosis and selection
components.selectionQuestion: Which option fits my situation after answering a sequence of questions?

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Answer branching questions to inspect a rule-based recommendation.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present demonstrates a path; Read lets the learner choose branches.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: A reached recommendation is not an assessment score.

components.summary: Sequence-builder reflection: learners put steps in the right order.

teaching.introduces: Make meaningful order and dependencies explicit by reconstructing an already-taught sequence.
teaching.exploration: Arrange supplied steps and check the authored order, then explain why that order matters.
teaching.evidence: Explicit checked attempts concern this sequence; dragging alone is engagement. Present demonstrates authored content with separate state; demonstrated answers are not learner attempts.
teaching.limits: Use a defensible order and teach the procedure first. Do not force one arbitrary ordering when several are valid, or infer general procedural skill from one solved puzzle.

components.mentalModel: Reconstructing order and procedure
components.selectionQuestion: Can I arrange the supplied steps into the correct sequence?

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Reconstruct the order of supplied steps and check the answer.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present demonstrates reconstruction; Read supports learner attempts.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Correctness concerns this authored sequence, not general mastery.

components.summary: Self-explanation reflection: learners complete sentence templates with chips.

teaching.introduces: Scaffold a coherent explanation using supplied concepts and sentence blanks, making relationships and reasoning visible.
teaching.exploration: Complete an explanation with authored chips, inspect feedback and articulate the resulting reasoning.
teaching.evidence: A checked completion supplies evidence for this constrained exercise, which is narrower than independently producing an explanation. Present demonstrates authored content with separate state; demonstrated answers are not learner attempts.
teaching.limits: Ground the template and solution in taught concepts. Preserve documented zones and chip references; do not claim automatic grading of arbitrary free-text reasoning.

components.mentalModel: Structured reasoning and explanation
components.selectionQuestion: Can I complete a sound explanation using the supplied concepts and sentence blanks?

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Complete an explanation from supplied concepts and sentence blanks.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present demonstrates a completed explanation; use Read for attempts.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Explicit results concern this exercise, not independent free-text reasoning.

components.summary: Knowledge-check section of multiple-choice questions.

teaching.introduces: Help learners apply taught knowledge, identify misconceptions and learn from answer-specific explanations.
teaching.exploration: Attempt a grounded question and inspect feedback that explains why alternatives are right or wrong.
teaching.evidence: Explicit learner answers and correctness concern the authored question. Present demonstrates authored content with separate state; demonstrated answers are not learner attempts.
teaching.limits: Teach or supply the required facts before assessing them. Use the existing single-correct-choice contract; do not invent partial-credit, free-text grading or general mastery guarantees.

components.mentalModel: Checking understanding and applying knowledge
components.selectionQuestion: Can I answer or apply what has already been taught?

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Submit an answer and inspect authored feedback.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present demonstrates answers; Read captures learner attempts.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Explicit correct/wrong attempts are evidence; views and stage demonstrations are not mastery.

components.summary: Introduce individual concepts and meanings, then practise recall with focused explanation cards. Examples and dialogue can clarify meaning; a flip records exposure, not correctness.

teaching.introduces: Introduce or recall one focused concept, term or question with a coherent explanation, example, dialogue or common mistake.
teaching.exploration: Attempt recall and reveal the explanation in Read; Present demonstrates the authored front and back.
teaching.evidence: A flip or view records exposure, not correctness or mastery. Use a grounded assessment when checked evidence is required.
teaching.limits: Keep one focused idea per card and use the existing word and definition fields. Use TextContent for connected explanation or TaxonomyBrowser to organize kinds; do not invent automatic recall grading.

components.mentalModel: Definitions, meaning, vocabulary and recall
components.selectionQuestion: What does this term or concept mean? Introduce or recall one focused idea per card, with a coherent explanation and concise example or dialogue. A flip is exposure, not correctness.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Try recall, then flip to inspect a definition or example.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Present demonstrates front/back; use Read for learner-controlled recall.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: A flip records exposure, not correctness of unauthored recall.

components.summary: Knowledge graph of concepts and the relations between them.

teaching.introduces: Introduce concepts and teach how they connect, depend on, support or differ from one another; a map can carry the main explanation.
teaching.exploration: Inspect named concepts, examples and labelled relationships; Present introduces groups and connections from the same authored graph.
teaching.evidence: A displayed map does not show that a learner can explain or reconstruct its relationships. Use a grounded response if needed.
teaching.limits: Label relationships precisely. Do not imply causation, sequence or equivalence through an unlabelled connection. TaxonomyBrowser organizes kinds; Flowchart traces a process. The current map is not automatically a matching exercise.

components.mentalModel: Relationships between concepts
components.selectionQuestion: How do ideas connect, depend on, support or differ from each other? Label the relationship explicitly.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Inspect concepts and their labelled relationships.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Check that labels and connections remain readable at phone width.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: A displayed relationship does not show the learner can explain it.

components.summary: Text block. Supports markdown. Optional size: "small" | "default" | "large" | "small-heavy" | "large-heavy".

teaching.introduces: Develop connected explanations, arguments, definitions, qualifications and concise supporting labels.
teaching.exploration: Read examples and follow reasoning with a clear hierarchy; use prose when its connections and nuance serve the goal.
teaching.evidence: Viewing, opening or selecting is engagement; ask for an observable explanation or application when the objective requires evidence.
teaching.limits: Keep the selected component’s role: TextContent supports Markdown prose; Text is a short line or metric. Labels and emphasis do not replace a missing mechanism, comparison or assessment.

components.mentalModel: Connected explanation and narrative
components.selectionQuestion: Does this idea need connected prose or narrative? Before choosing TextContent, consider comparisons, diagrams, tables or charts; use prose when it best teaches the goal.

learningBehavior.learnerAction: Read a connected explanation or argument.
learningBehavior.presentationConstraint: Keep prose readable in Read and Present; check long paragraphs at phone width.
learningBehavior.evidenceBoundary: Prose can be the right representation; viewing it is not assessment.

components.summary: Plain text line with optional subtext. variant 'number' uses tabular number styling; subtextVariant 'metric' colors a leading +/- subtext green/red.

teaching.exploration: Trace the code and connect each relevant part to its behavior, assumptions and expected result.

teaching.limits: A code block is a display, not a runtime. Do not claim execution, tests or benchmarks without an actual supported environment and evidence; keep examples current and source-grounded.

components.summary: A drawing written as inline SVG markup (one <svg viewBox="…"> element), with an optional caption under it. Color names of the Loom palette (blue, peach, green, mauve, red, yellow, teal, text, subtext0, overlay1, surface0, …) follow the theme; shapes without a fill take the text color. teaching.introduces: Explain spatial structure, anatomy, a mechanism, geometry or a clearly labelled analogy.
teaching.exploration: Inspect labelled parts and relationships; supported shape IDs can focus narration on meaningful details.
teaching.evidence: Viewing, opening or selecting is engagement; ask for an observable explanation or application when the objective requires evidence.
teaching.limits: Label conceptual or not-to-scale drawings when needed. Keep figures readable and accessible; do not use arbitrary geometry as measured evidence or assume a drawing executes the represented system.
